prompt.en: A voice signal is loud on the meter but clipped and hard to understand. Which report habit best separates the observations?

text.en: Give a strong strength number but describe the readability problem instead of pretending loud means clear.
Always give the highest readability whenever the S-meter is high.
Add a tone digit because distorted voice must be reported like keyed Morse.
Report only transmitter power because reception reports are about watts.

explanation.en: Readability and strength are separate parts of a report. A loud signal can still be difficult to copy if the audio is poor.

prompt.en: Which statement is NOT true about the Q signals taught in this lesson?

text.en: Adding a question mark can turn a Q signal into a request rather than a statement.
QRN points to static-type trouble rather than another station deliberately occupying the channel.
QSY can be used when stations agree to move frequency.
The question mark is decorative and never changes the job of a Q signal.

explanation.en: In operating practice, the question form matters. For example, a busy-frequency check is different from simply stating a condition.

prompt.en: An S-meter rises one unit during a period of obvious fading, and the distant operator says their transmitter power did not change. What conclusion best fits the lesson?

text.en: Do not calculate transmitter power from that jump; the path changed, so the simple power comparison is not controlled.
The transmitter power must have quadrupled even though the operator reports no change.
The tone digit of the RST report must improve whenever fading raises the meter.
The receiver should report QRN because any meter movement is static.

explanation.en: The S-unit power relationship is a simplified comparison when other conditions remain steady. Fading changes the path, so the meter movement is not proof of a transmitter-power change.
